extracted.intended_audience: writers of narrative prose; readers of Slate Book Review interested in craft
extracted.subtask_description: Critical summary of Ursula K. Le Guin's practical guidelines for writing narrative prose — emphasizing sentence-level choices, punctuation, rhythm, and sustaining story/movement. Aimed at practicing (not beginner) writers who want to sharpen awareness of prose techniques and storytelling decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know what you're doing with your language and why
rubrics_metrics.description: “The important thing for a writer … is to know what you're doing with your language and why.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Le Guin urges writers to have explicit reasons for stylistic choices rather than following rules blindly. This includes choosing clarity and ensuring readers will know what you mean; writers may disagree with her stated reasons but should form some rationale for each choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writer's moral duty to use language thoughtfully and well
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is ‘a writer's moral duty … to use language thoughtfully and well.’”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not merely correctness: this covers clarity, care, and respect for readers. The reviewer notes Le Guin stresses responsibility in language-use as part of craft and ethical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'fake rules' and arbitrary dicta
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject wonky, almost inexplicable principles such as the idea that sentences shouldn’t begin with the construction 'There is.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Le Guin calls out pedagogical shortcuts that masquerade as rules; instead of memorizing prohibitions, understand the effect of constructions so you can choose intentionally. Fake rules are pedagogical failure and should be unlearned.

rubrics_metrics.name: The chief duty of a narrative sentence: keep the story going
rubrics_metrics.description: “The chief duty of a narrative sentence is to keep the story going.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every sentence should serve narrative momentum rather than pausing for ornament or exposition. This principle grounds other choices (e.g., tense, punctuation, word order) — prefer options that maintain flow and forward movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize movement/action over static description
rubrics_metrics.description: Make exercises and prose 'not a static scene but the account of an act or action, something happening.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Le Guin recommends rendering scenes as events that change something; prose should convey action and transformation. Anti-pattern: static tableaux that don't advance plot, character, or change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let ornate prose stop the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Ornate, elaborate prose that causes readers to 'stop to be admired' interrupts narrative and is a flaw in narrative prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While poetic language can invite admiration, in narrative prose excessive ornament can remove readers from the story. Use elegance selectively; avoid phrasing that consistently makes readers pause and admire style at the expense of story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid frequent tense shifts
rubrics_metrics.description: Changing verb tense too often interrupts the flow of a story, pulling the reader out of its spell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain tense consistency unless there is a clear narrative purpose for shifts. Tense changes are an anti-pattern that damage narrative continuity and reader immersion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation and grammar are tools; learn their differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Periods, semicolons, commas and their kin are to a writer as tools are to a laborer; a writer who doesn't know them is like a carpenter who doesn't know a hammer from a screwdriver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand the functions and effects of punctuation marks so you can deploy them intentionally to shape rhythm, emphasis, and clarity. Ignorance of these tools undermines craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use repetition, adjectives, and adverbs with purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapters address practical topics—'Repetition,' 'Adjectives and Adverbs'—implying close, purposeful attention to these elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat modifiers and repeated elements as deliberate choices that affect pace, emphasis, and tone. Overuse or careless repetition is an anti-pattern; use them to reinforce rather than clutter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train craft via constrained exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercises instruct readers to restrict prose in particular ways (e.g., 'Write a paragraph of narrative … in sentences of seven or fewer words' or 'Write a half page to a page of narrative … that is all one sentence').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Le Guin favors practice through formal constraints to heighten awareness of sentence-level effects. The book provides minimal procedural detail, focusing instead on how to read and think about the product of the constraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let the text 'do its own work' and breathe/grow
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing is a kind of work about letting the text do its own work, letting it breathe and grow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate drafts and revisions that allow the writing to develop organically; avoid forcing effects that stifle the text's internal dynamics. The reviewer notes Le Guin encourages hands-on practice rather than abstract rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: This guide is not for beginners
rubrics_metrics.description: The book hedges from the first pages, insisting 'it is not a book for beginners.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect material aimed at writers with some experience. The book's purpose is to 'clarify and intensify your awareness' of prose elements rather than teach basic composition from scratch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on reading and thinking about finished exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: Le Guin offers only the bare minimum of information about how to complete exercises, often focusing far more on how to read and think about the finished products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pedagogical value comes from analyzing outcomes and developing critical awareness, not from detailed step-by-step instructions. Use the exercises as prompts for reflection on effect and reader experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid treating writing primarily as self-expression or therapy
rubrics_metrics.description: Le Guin 'refuses to discuss writing as self-expression, as therapy, or as a spiritual adventure.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize craft, story, and reader experience rather than introspective or therapeutic aims. This is a normative stance: writing should be judged by how it moves readers and advances narrative, not solely by the writer's personal catharsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to word choice and etymology to shape effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Le Guin, in A Wizard of Earthsea, 'relies heavily on words with Germanic roots to convey the rawness of her windswept world.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select words (including attention to their roots and connotations) to produce wanted tonal and world-building effects. Word etymology and register are deliberate levers for mood and texture.
